screens.title: Monitoring System Performance
screens.narratorSegment: Monitoring system performance is about more than watching numbers. It is about learning what normal looks like, spotting deviations quickly, and identifying whether the problem lives in C P U, memory, disk, or network. In this lesson you will learn the purpose and meaning of the core metrics: C P U user and wait time, memory used versus available, disk utilization and queue lengths, and socket states. You will also become familiar with the primary tools that reveal these metrics. For example, vmstat gives a live, concise view of C P U, memory, and IO activity; iostat dives into device-level input and output metrics like await and percent utilization; free -h summarizes memory and available space; sar collects historical samples for trend analysis; and ss shows active socket states. By the end, you will know which tool to reach for first when a system is slow, how to interpret a high wa or a high avgqu-sz, and how to set a baseline so you can detect anomalies. As you watch the cards on this slide, imagine a service that suddenly becomes slow — the right metric will point you to C P U saturation, swapping, disk saturation, or network connection storms.

screens.title: What to measure: CPU, Memory, Disk, Network
screens.narratorSegment: A first, practical definition: C P U utilization measures how much time the processor spends doing work, often split into user and system time, with idle and iowait showing how much time the C P U has nothing to do or is waiting for input and output. Memory usage describes how much physical R A M is in use, how much is used for buffers and cache, and how much is truly available to applications; swap and available tell the real story about memory pressure. Disk input and output is measured by read/write rates, queue depth, and service times; high percent utilization and long waits indicate the disk cannot keep up. Network health is revealed by socket counts and connection states; many incomplete handshakes can point to attacks or application issues. Each metric answers a different question: is the C P U busy, are we running out of R A M, is the disk saturated, or is the network congested? A common misconception is to treat low free memory as a problem; in Linux, buffers and cache are used intentionally and can be freed if processes need R A M. Another trap is blaming C P U for slowness when the real cause is iowait — the processor appears idle while waiting for disk. A quick example: a web service that responds slowly while CPUs are mostly idle but wa is high suggests disk or storage latency, not compute. The takeaway: measure the right metric for the symptom and avoid misreading caches and idle time.

keyIdea.text: Match the symptom to the metric: time waiting for I/O is not CPU saturation, low free memory is not always memory shortage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › What to measure
Definitions
Short, practical definitions you can remember under pressure.
  • CPU: user/system/idle/iowait — high iowait points to I/O latency.
  • Memory: total/used/buff-cache/available — available is the reliable indicator of free RAM.
  • Disk I/O: throughput, avg queue size, await, %util — these show device saturation.
  • Network: socket states and counts — incomplete handshakes or many CLOSE_WAIT states reveal issues.
Key Takeaway

Always interpret one metric in context with others; a slow service often shows a telltale combination such as high wa with low CPU usage.

Concrete example
Consider a web server where users report latency. top shows CPU at 10% idle, but vmstat shows wa at 30%. iostat shows %util near 100% and await high for the primary device. Conclusion: the storage subsystem is the bottleneck, not CPU load. Fixes may include tuning IO scheduling, adding faster storage, or moving hotspots off the device.
Misconception
Low free memory equals out of memory. Not true — Linux uses RAM for cache by design.
Pro tip
Use the available column in free and the wa column in vmstat for practical interpretation.

screens.title: Using vmstat for live system snapshots
screens.narratorSegment: vmstat is your quick snapshot and short-term trend tool. Run vmstat with an interval and count, for example vmstat 1 5, to get continuous samples. The procs section reports runnable and blocked processes, which tells you if processes are C P U-bound or waiting for resources. In memory, swpd shows swap used, free is available free R A M, buff and cache show kernel buffers and page cache. In swap, si and so are swap in and swap out activity — significant si/so indicates memory pressure. The io columns bi and bo reflect block reads and writes; a sustained high of either with rising wa suggests storage load. System columns show interrupts and context switches; sudden jumps can indicate device or driver work. In C P U, us and sy are C P U time spent in user and kernel code, id is idle, and wa is time waiting on input and output. A concrete command example is vmstat 1 10 while you run a load generator. A common mistake is to panic at low free memory without checking buff/cache and available. To practice, run vmstat before, during, and after a stress tool and watch how si/so and wa move. The core skill is mapping changes back to the action that caused them.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › vmstat walkthrough
Run and read vmstat
Use an interval to see how numbers change under load.
  • si/so: swapping in/out — memory pressure if nonzero and sustained.
  • wa: CPU waiting for I/O — points to disk issues when high.
  • procs r: runnable processes — indicates CPU demand.
Check your understanding
If wa rises when you run a disk write dd, what is the likely bottleneck?
Example
Run vmstat 1 10 while generating load; watch us, sy, id, wa and si/so shift as processes compete for CPU and IO.
Command and sample output (illustrative)
vmstat 1 5
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
 1  0      0 1024000 200000 1500000    0    0     0     0  100  200 10  5 85  0
 2  0      0  500000 200000 1500000  100  200 5000 1000  250  400 20 10 50 20 0
Interpretation
  • Line one: normal since-boot summary. Line two: under load — si/so show swapping, bi/bo large, wa increased.
  • If await increases in iostat when wa is high, the disk is the likely bottleneck.
  • Don’t treat buff/cache as lost memory; check available instead.

screens.title: iostat metrics: await, svctm, avgqu-sz, %util
screens.narratorSegment: iostat -x gives extended device metrics that explain how busy and how congested a storage device is. The primary values to watch are %util, avgqu-sz, await, and svctm. Percent utilization shows the fraction of time the device was busy; near 100% means the device had no idle time and may be a bottleneck. Avgqu-sz is the average queue length of outstanding input and output requests — a growing queue means the device cannot service requests fast enough. Await is the average time a request spends waiting plus service time; svctm is the average service time only. When await is much larger than svctm, most of the time is spent waiting in queue rather than being serviced, showing contention. For example, a disk showing %util at 100, avgqu-sz of 10, await 50ms, and svctm 5ms clearly indicates queued requests and long waits. A common misunderstanding is to treat svctm alone as the whole story; svctm can be low while await is high if queueing dominates. In practice you should look for combinations: high %util plus high avgqu-sz and await point firmly to a device-level bottleneck. The practical response is to reduce load, improve concurrency limits, or provision faster storage.

keyIdea.text: Look for the trio: high %util, growing avgqu-sz, and await much higher than svctm to confirm disk contention.

content.html:
iostat › Chapter 4.2 › Disk metrics comparison
Metric definitions
  • %util: percentage of time the disk was busy.
  • avgqu-sz: average queue length of I/O requests.
  • await: average wait time including queuing.
  • svctm: average service time only.
Common patterns
- %util near 100 with high avgqu-sz and await: device saturated.
- High await but low svctm: queuing is the main issue.
Example device output
Device    r/s    w/s    rkB/s  wkB/s  avgqu-sz  await  svctm  %util
sdb      50.0  200.0  1000.0 4000.0    10.0    50.0   5.0   100.0
Interpretation: avg queue 10, await 50ms vs svctm 5ms, util 100% — this device is a bottleneck.
Misread
Don’t assume svctm alone defines performance; compare await and svctm to see queueing impact.

screens.title: Understanding free -h and buff/cache
screens.narratorSegment: free -h gives a quick snapshot of total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available memory. The critical column to rely on is available: it estimates how much memory can be given to new processes without swapping. Buff/cache represents memory used by the kernel for file caches and buffers; Linux keeps this memory populated to speed IO, and it is freed when applications need R A M. A common mistake is to treat buff/cache as wasted memory — in fact, unused R A M is wasted opportunity, so the kernel favors using free R A M for cache. If available is consistently low and swap usage (swpd) climbs, your system is under memory pressure. For example, run free -h before and during a memory hogging test; you will see available drop and swpd increase if swapping is triggered. Also note shared represents memory shared between processes and is less useful for judging pressure. When teaching teams, emphasize the behavior: cache helps performance and should not be cleared as a knee-jerk reaction. Instead, investigate which processes consume memory and consider capacity planning or memory-limiting containers. The takeaway is to use available and swap activity as your primary indicators of memory health.

keyIdea.title: Memory diagnosis
keyIdea.text: Buff/cache is not a problem by itself — watch available and swap activity to detect real memory pressure.

content.html:
free -h › Chapter 4.2 › Memory snapshot
Read free -h
Focus on total, available, buff/cache, and swpd.
              total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           8Gi       5.2Gi       200Mi        60Mi       2.6Gi       2.1Gi
Swap:          2Gi         0Gi         2Gi
In this example available is 2.1Gi — the realistic free memory for new apps. Buff/cache is 2.6Gi and will be freed when needed. Swap is unused here.
Practical tip
Avoid clearing cache to 'free' memory; find memory-hungry processes or add RAM if available is consistently low.
Check
If available is low and swpd > 0, you have memory pressure and should investigate process usage or limits.

screens.title: Using sar for historical analysis
screens.narratorSegment: sar is the System Activity Reporter and is designed for collecting metrics over time and reading historical files. It is part of the sysstat package and, when enabled, writes periodic snapshots to files, typically under /var/log/sa. Use sar -u to read C P U usage history, sar -r for memory, and sar -b for block device statistics. The power of sar is its ability to replay a day’s worth of samples so you can locate when a spike occurred and correlate across subsystems. For example, sar -f /var/log/sa/sa10 will replay activity recorded on day 10. In practice, enable sysstat on production hosts you need to analyze historically, and use sar to establish baselines and to answer questions like: did a spike in disk waits precede a service outage? The common misuse is relying only on live commands; without history you may miss intermittent issues. A simple process is: enable collection, reproduce or wait for an event, then use sar filters to extract the window of interest and compare C P U, memory, and device metrics together. That comparison is how you discover whether a past slowdown was caused by sustained swap activity, a transient input and output storm, or an increase in context switches. The takeaway: sar turns short-term observability into forensic evidence.

content.html:
sar › Chapter 4.2 › Historical analysis
Collect and replay
Enable sysstat to gather samples, then use sar to analyze windows of interest.
# Read CPU history sar -u 1 5 # Read data from a saved day file sar -f /var/log/sa/sa10
Use sar to correlate spikes across CPU, memory, and device metrics and to answer when an incident began and how long it lasted.
Why it matters
Transient issues are common; without historical data you may never explain an intermittent slowdown.
Pro tip
Store sar data long enough to capture business cycles and typical peak windows for accurate baselines.

screens.title: Inspecting network state with ss
screens.narratorSegment: ss is the modern, faster replacement for netstat and provides detailed socket information. Use ss -tulpn to list listening TCP and UDP sockets and the processes that own them. ss -s gives a compact summary of socket states, and ss -ti gives detailed TCP info including retransmits and congestion control. When investigating network-related slowness, look for unexpectedly many connections in SYN_RECV, which can indicate half-open connections or an incoming flood, and many CLOSE_WAIT states, which can indicate an application not closing sockets properly. A concrete use case: a server reports high connection latency and a glance at ss -s shows thousands of connections in SYN_RECV — this suggests the server is under a connection attack or the network stack is overloaded, not an application compute problem. Another situation: many CLOSE_WAIT entries point to the application failing to close sockets; fixing the code or adjusting timeouts resolves the issue. ss is fast and scriptable, so include it in automated checks. Remember to combine network inspection with system metrics: socket storms often show up as increased interrupts or context switches in vmstat and sar. The takeaway is to use ss to map connection states to application behavior and to distinguish network-layer problems from C P U or disk causes.

content.html:
ss › Chapter 4.2 › Socket inspection
Common ss commands
Quick commands to locate problematic states and listening processes.
ss -tulpn   # listening sockets and processes
ss -s       # socket summary
ss -ti      # detailed TCP info
Example scenarios
  • Many SYN_RECV: incomplete handshakes — possible flood or network issue.
  • Many CLOSE_WAIT: application not closing sockets — investigate code or increase timeouts.
  • High socket counts: correlate with CPU interrupts and context switches for impact.
Tip
Combine ss with vmstat or sar to see if a socket event caused CPU or IO spikes.

screens.title: Systematic troubleshooting workflow
screens.narratorSegment: When performance degrades, follow a repeatable workflow: establish the symptom, collect current metrics, and then drill down with the right tool. First, ask: is the system C P U-bound, memory-starved, IO-saturated, or network-constrained? Start with top or htop to find immediate resource consumers and then run vmstat for a concise multi-metric view. If vmstat shows high wa, move to iostat -x to inspect device-level await and %util. If swpd is increasing or available memory is low, use free -h and inspect the largest processes. For historical context or intermittent issues, consult sar data. If network issues are suspected, run ss to inspect connection states. Always capture a baseline before changes so you can revert and compare. A concrete example: users report slow response; top shows low C P U usage but vmstat shows high wa; iostat shows %util at 100 and avgqu-sz growing — the workflow points to a disk bottleneck. Common mistakes include jumping to resizing resources without checking whether the bottleneck is actually elsewhere, or changing scheduling and cache settings without reproducing the problem under controlled load. The workflow ends with an action and verification: apply a fix or mitigation and observe the same metrics to confirm improvement.

Workflow › Chapter 4.2 › Troubleshooting
Repeatable steps
  1. Observe symptom and get baseline (top, vmstat).
  2. Hypothesize the subsystem (CPU / memory / disk / network).
  3. Probe with targeted tool (iostat, free, sar, ss).
  4. Apply mitigation and verify by re-measuring.
Example
High latency with low CPU but high wa → iostat shows disk saturated → mitigate by reducing I/O concurrency or moving hot data.
Checklist while troubleshooting
Baseline
Capture normal vmstat/iostat/free samples before changes.
Reproduce
If safe, generate targeted load to observe metric shifts.
Verify
After any change, re-run the same commands to confirm improvement or regression.

screens.title: Lab walkthrough: generating CPU, disk, and memory load
screens.narratorSegment: The lab walkthrough demonstrates how to generate controlled load and watch the monitoring tools respond. Start by opening two terminals. In terminal A run vmstat 1 10 and iostat -x 1 10 to sample baseline metrics. In terminal B you will create load. For C P U stress, install stress and run stress -c 2 -t 30s to load two cores for 30 seconds; observe vmstat’s us rising and id falling. For disk input and output, run dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile bs=1M count=1000 oflag=direct & to create sustained writes; watch iostat percent utilization and await grow and vmstat wa increase. For memory pressure, run a small Python allocation that holds memory, for example Python three -c "a = 'x' * (512**3); input('Press Enter')" & adjusted to your system; observe free -h available decreasing and potentially swpd increasing. Always run these tests on a safe non-production environment and remember to kill background processes and remove tempfile when finished. The lab shows how particular columns react: us/sy/id for C P U, wa/si/so for VM and swap, %util/avgqu-sz/await for disks. This exercise trains your eye to correlate cause and effect in real time.

Lab › Chapter 4.2 › Load generation
Starter commands
# Terminal A: observe vmstat 1 10 iostat -x 1 10 free -h ss -s # Terminal B: generate CPU load sudo apt install stress stress -c 2 -t 30s # Disk write load dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile bs=1M count=1000 oflag=direct & # Memory allocation (adjust size safely) python3 -c "a = 'x' * (512**3); input('Press Enter to release')" &
Observe the shifting columns and record the timeline. Always clean up: kill background jobs and remove tempfile.
Expected reactions
- CPU stress: vmstat us increases, id drops.
- Disk dd: iostat %util and await increase, vmstat wa rises.
- Memory allocation: free available drops, swpd may rise if under pressure.
Safety
Run tests on a non-production host. Monitor and stop the test if system responsiveness collapses.

screens.title: Interpreting vmstat and iostat sample outputs
screens.narratorSegment: Here is a worked example to build diagnostic reasoning. You are given vmstat showing a drop in free memory, si and so both nonzero, bi high, and C P U wa rising. Next, iostat shows a device with %util at 100, avgqu-sz at 10, await 50ms and svctm 5ms. Step one: read vmstat — nonzero si/so indicates swapping, which often happens when available memory is insufficient. High bi suggests heavy block reads. The rising wa in vmstat indicates the C P U is spending more time waiting for input and output. Step two: read iostat — %util at 100 with avgqu-sz and await large means the disk is saturated and requests are queuing. Step three: combine signals — swapping generates more disk input and output which increases queueing and thus wa; it creates a feedback loop. The correct diagnosis is memory pressure causing swapping that triggers disk saturation. A common wrong conclusion would be to blame C P U or network. The right remediation sequence is to stop memory-heavy processes, add R A M, or move workload and then re-measure. Finally, verify the fix by rerunning the same vmstat and iostat checks to confirm si/so and await decreased. This methodical reasoning is what the assessment expects.

procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----

screens.title: Cleanup and verification after load tests
screens.narratorSegment: After running load tests or making configuration changes, it is essential to stop test processes, remove temporary files, and verify the system returned to baseline. First, identify background test jobs with ps and kill them or use pkill for known process names. Remove any temporary files created by dd to avoid prolonged disk pressure. Next, rerun vmstat and iostat samples to confirm that us, wa, si/so, avgqu-sz and %util returned to expected baseline values. If you made a change intended to reduce input and output, you should see await and avgqu-sz drop. If you increased R A M or limited memory use, available memory should rise and swpd should fall. For historical confirmation, check sar logs for the trend window covering your tests. A common oversight is to leave test workloads running or to forget tempfile removal, which will bias future baselines. Finally, document the before and after samples as part of your change record so you can show that the mitigation had the intended effect. This verification step ensures that your tests and fixes are responsible and reversible. Cleanup and verification after load tests means always revert test changes and confirm metric recovery; verification documents the success of your mitigation.. In practical terms, how to return to baseline and confirm improvements. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cleanup checklist

screens.narratorSegment: This timeline gives a compact 15-minute plan to run the live lab. Minute 0–2: capture baseline samples using vmstat 1 10, iostat -x 1 10, free -h and ss -s. Minute 2–6: generate C P U load with stress -c 2 -t 30s and observe vmstat and free for C P U and memory changes. Minute 6–10: generate disk load with dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile bs=1M count=1000 oflag=direct & and watch iostat metrics change, especially %util, avgqu-sz and await; observe vmstat wa. fullNarratorScript:
Monitoring system performance is about more than watching numbers. It is about learning what normal looks like, spotting deviations quickly, and identifying whether the problem lives in C P U, memory, disk, or network. In this lesson you will learn the purpose and meaning of the core metrics: C P U user and wait time, memory used versus available, disk utilization and queue lengths, and socket states. You will also become familiar with the primary tools that reveal these metrics. For example, vmstat gives a live, concise view of C P U, memory, and IO activity; iostat dives into device-level input and output metrics like await and percent utilization; free -h summarizes memory and available space; sar collects historical samples for trend analysis; and ss shows active socket states. By the end, you will know which tool to reach for first when a system is slow, how to interpret a high wa or a high avgqu-sz, and how to set a baseline so you can detect anomalies. As you watch the cards on this slide, imagine a service that suddenly becomes slow — the right metric will point you to C P U saturation, swapping, disk saturation, or network connection storms.

By the end of this chapter you will identify core system performance metrics, run the appropriate Linux tools to observe them, and interpret outputs to find bottlenecks. Objective one focuses on recognizing C P U, memory, disk, and network metrics and understanding what a high or low value actually implies. Objective two centers on vmstat: you will run repeated samples, read the procs, memory, swap, io, system, and C P U columns, and know which numbers suggest disk wait or swapping. Objective three covers iostat and free: you will use iostat -x to read percent utilization, queue lengths, await, and service time, and you will use free -h to interpret total, used, buff/cache and available so that you do not mistake cache for a shortage. Objective four introduces sar and ss: you will collect historical samples with sar for trend analysis and use ss to inspect active socket states to find networking causes. Each objective pairs a command with a practical reason — this ensures you can run, read, and act on the data during live troubleshooting.

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on skills. You will practice reading live vmstat samples to spot rising wa values and swap activity, run iostat -x to evaluate %util and await on specific devices, and use free -h to separate buff/cache from truly available memory. You will also gather historical data with sar and replay logs to find when a past incident began. On the networking side, you will use ss -tulpn to identify listening sockets and ss -s to read socket summary statistics. The lab will have concrete commands to produce C P U, disk, and memory load so you can observe changes in the exact columns we discuss. Understanding how outputs change under load helps you distinguish a real bottleneck from normal variability. Finally, you will practice a cleanup step: stopping stressors and removing temporary files so your baseline returns to normal. These are repeatable workflows you can apply to production or test systems safely.

A first, practical definition: C P U utilization measures how much time the processor spends doing work, often split into user and system time, with idle and iowait showing how much time the C P U has nothing to do or is waiting for input and output. Memory usage describes how much physical R A M is in use, how much is used for buffers and cache, and how much is truly available to applications; swap and available tell the real story about memory pressure. Disk input and output is measured by read/write rates, queue depth, and service times; high percent utilization and long waits indicate the disk cannot keep up. Network health is revealed by socket counts and connection states; many incomplete handshakes can point to attacks or application issues. Each metric answers a different question: is the C P U busy, are we running out of R A M, is the disk saturated, or is the network congested? A common misconception is to treat low free memory as a problem; in Linux, buffers and cache are used intentionally and can be freed if processes need R A M. Another trap is blaming C P U for slowness when the real cause is iowait — the processor appears idle while waiting for disk. A quick example: a web service that responds slowly while CPUs are mostly idle but wa is high suggests disk or storage latency, not compute. The takeaway: measure the right metric for the symptom and avoid misreading caches and idle time.

vmstat is your quick snapshot and short-term trend tool. Run vmstat with an interval and count, for example vmstat 1 5, to get continuous samples. The procs section reports runnable and blocked processes, which tells you if processes are C P U-bound or waiting for resources. In memory, swpd shows swap used, free is available free R A M, buff and cache show kernel buffers and page cache. In swap, si and so are swap in and swap out activity — significant si/so indicates memory pressure. The io columns bi and bo reflect block reads and writes; a sustained high of either with rising wa suggests storage load. System columns show interrupts and context switches; sudden jumps can indicate device or driver work. In C P U, us and sy are C P U time spent in user and kernel code, id is idle, and wa is time waiting on input and output. A concrete command example is vmstat 1 10 while you run a load generator. A common mistake is to panic at low free memory without checking buff/cache and available. To practice, run vmstat before, during, and after a stress tool and watch how si/so and wa move. The core skill is mapping changes back to the action that caused them.

iostat -x gives extended device metrics that explain how busy and how congested a storage device is. The primary values to watch are %util, avgqu-sz, await, and svctm. Percent utilization shows the fraction of time the device was busy; near 100% means the device had no idle time and may be a bottleneck. Avgqu-sz is the average queue length of outstanding input and output requests — a growing queue means the device cannot service requests fast enough. Await is the average time a request spends waiting plus service time; svctm is the average service time only. When await is much larger than svctm, most of the time is spent waiting in queue rather than being serviced, showing contention. For example, a disk showing %util at 100, avgqu-sz of 10, await 50ms, and svctm 5ms clearly indicates queued requests and long waits. A common misunderstanding is to treat svctm alone as the whole story; svctm can be low while await is high if queueing dominates. In practice you should look for combinations: high %util plus high avgqu-sz and await point firmly to a device-level bottleneck. The practical response is to reduce load, improve concurrency limits, or provision faster storage.

free -h gives a quick snapshot of total, used, free, shared, buff/cache, and available memory. The critical column to rely on is available: it estimates how much memory can be given to new processes without swapping. Buff/cache represents memory used by the kernel for file caches and buffers; Linux keeps this memory populated to speed IO, and it is freed when applications need R A M. A common mistake is to treat buff/cache as wasted memory — in fact, unused R A M is wasted opportunity, so the kernel favors using free R A M for cache. If available is consistently low and swap usage (swpd) climbs, your system is under memory pressure. For example, run free -h before and during a memory hogging test; you will see available drop and swpd increase if swapping is triggered. Also note shared represents memory shared between processes and is less useful for judging pressure. When teaching teams, emphasize the behavior: cache helps performance and should not be cleared as a knee-jerk reaction. Instead, investigate which processes consume memory and consider capacity planning or memory-limiting containers. The takeaway is to use available and swap activity as your primary indicators of memory health.

sar is the System Activity Reporter and is designed for collecting metrics over time and reading historical files. It is part of the sysstat package and, when enabled, writes periodic snapshots to files, typically under /var/log/sa. Use sar -u to read C P U usage history, sar -r for memory, and sar -b for block device statistics. The power of sar is its ability to replay a day’s worth of samples so you can locate when a spike occurred and correlate across subsystems. For example, sar -f /var/log/sa/sa10 will replay activity recorded on day 10. In practice, enable sysstat on production hosts you need to analyze historically, and use sar to establish baselines and to answer questions like: did a spike in disk waits precede a service outage? The common misuse is relying only on live commands; without history you may miss intermittent issues. A simple process is: enable collection, reproduce or wait for an event, then use sar filters to extract the window of interest and compare C P U, memory, and device metrics together. That comparison is how you discover whether a past slowdown was caused by sustained swap activity, a transient input and output storm, or an increase in context switches. The takeaway: sar turns short-term observability into forensic evidence.

ss is the modern, faster replacement for netstat and provides detailed socket information. Use ss -tulpn to list listening TCP and UDP sockets and the processes that own them. ss -s gives a compact summary of socket states, and ss -ti gives detailed TCP info including retransmits and congestion control. When investigating network-related slowness, look for unexpectedly many connections in SYN_RECV, which can indicate half-open connections or an incoming flood, and many CLOSE_WAIT states, which can indicate an application not closing sockets properly. A concrete use case: a server reports high connection latency and a glance at ss -s shows thousands of connections in SYN_RECV — this suggests the server is under a connection attack or the network stack is overloaded, not an application compute problem. Another situation: many CLOSE_WAIT entries point to the application failing to close sockets; fixing the code or adjusting timeouts resolves the issue. ss is fast and scriptable, so include it in automated checks. Remember to combine network inspection with system metrics: socket storms often show up as increased interrupts or context switches in vmstat and sar. The takeaway is to use ss to map connection states to application behavior and to distinguish network-layer problems from C P U or disk causes.

When performance degrades, follow a repeatable workflow: establish the symptom, collect current metrics, and then drill down with the right tool. First, ask: is the system C P U-bound, memory-starved, IO-saturated, or network-constrained? Start with top or htop to find immediate resource consumers and then run vmstat for a concise multi-metric view. If vmstat shows high wa, move to iostat -x to inspect device-level await and %util. If swpd is increasing or available memory is low, use free -h and inspect the largest processes. For historical context or intermittent issues, consult sar data. If network issues are suspected, run ss to inspect connection states. Always capture a baseline before changes so you can revert and compare. A concrete example: users report slow response; top shows low C P U usage but vmstat shows high wa; iostat shows %util at 100 and avgqu-sz growing — the workflow points to a disk bottleneck. Common mistakes include jumping to resizing resources without checking whether the bottleneck is actually elsewhere, or changing scheduling and cache settings without reproducing the problem under controlled load. The lab walkthrough demonstrates how to generate controlled load and watch the monitoring tools respond. Start by opening two terminals. In terminal A run vmstat 1 10 and iostat -x 1 10 to sample baseline metrics. In terminal B you will create load. For C P U stress, install stress and run stress -c 2 -t 30s to load two cores for 30 seconds; observe vmstat’s us rising and id falling. For disk input and output, run dd if=/dev/zero of=tempfile bs=1M count=1000 oflag=direct & to create sustained writes; watch iostat percent utilization and await grow and vmstat wa increase. For memory pressure, run a small Python allocation that holds memory, for example Python three -c "a = 'x' * (512**3); input('Press Enter')" & adjusted to your system; observe free -h available decreasing and potentially swpd increasing. Always run these tests on a safe non-production environment and remember to kill background processes and remove tempfile when finished. The lab shows how particular columns react: us/sy/id for C P U, wa/si/so for VM and swap, %util/avgqu-sz/await for disks. This exercise trains your eye to correlate cause and effect in real time.

Here is a worked example to build diagnostic reasoning. You are given vmstat showing a drop in free memory, si and so both nonzero, bi high, and C P U wa rising. Next, iostat shows a device with %util at 100, avgqu-sz at 10, await 50ms and svctm 5ms. Step one: read vmstat — nonzero si/so indicates swapping, which often happens when available memory is insufficient. High bi suggests heavy block reads. The rising wa in vmstat indicates the C P U is spending more time waiting for input and output. Step two: read iostat — %util at 100 with avgqu-sz and await large means the disk is saturated and requests are queuing. Step three: combine signals — swapping generates more disk input and output which increases queueing and thus wa; it creates a feedback loop. The correct diagnosis is memory pressure causing swapping that triggers disk saturation. A common wrong conclusion would be to blame C P U or network. The right remediation sequence is to stop memory-heavy processes, add R A M, or move workload and then re-measure. Finally, verify the fix by rerunning the same vmstat and iostat checks to confirm si/so and await decreased. This methodical reasoning is what the assessment expects.

After running load tests or making configuration changes, it is essential to stop test processes, remove temporary files, and verify the system returned to baseline. First, identify background test jobs with ps and kill them or use pkill for known process names. Remove any temporary files created by dd to avoid prolonged disk pressure. Next, rerun vmstat and iostat samples to confirm that us, wa, si/so, avgqu-sz and %util returned to expected baseline values. If you made a change intended to reduce input and output, you should see await and avgqu-sz drop. If you increased R A M or limited memory use, available memory should rise and swpd should fall. For historical confirmation, check sar logs for the trend window covering your tests. A common oversight is to leave test workloads running or to forget tempfile removal, which will bias future baselines. Finally, document the before and after samples as part of your change record so you can show that the mitigation had the intended effect. This verification step ensures that your tests and fixes are responsible and reversible. These three compact ideas summarize practical monitoring: First, map symptoms to the correct metric. High iowait means look at disk metrics; high swap and low available memory means memory pressure. Second, use the right tool for the job: vmstat for quick multi-metric live sampling, iostat for device-level input and output detail, free -h for memory snapshot, sar for history, and ss for socket state. Third, use a repeatable workflow: observe, hypothesize, probe with the targeted tool, apply a mitigation, and verify using the same metrics. Each concept reduces false positives and helps you act efficiently under pressure. Keep these in mind as you perform the lab and when you return to production troubleshooting.
